lead: Replace the diodes of a rectifier with thyristors and every turn-on can be delayed by a firing angle α. The average output then falls as α grows, and with a load that keeps current flowing it can even turn negative. Battery chargers, DC motor drives and electrolysis supplies work this way. This chapter covers the one-pulse (half-wave), half-controlled and fully controlled two-pulse circuits with R, RL and RLE loads, and when the current is continuous.
prereq: You need: thyristor turn-on by a gate pulse and turn-off at current zero, from the power semiconductor devices topic, and the diode circuits of diode rectifiers.

sections.h3: Firing angle and the half-wave controlled rectifier

blocks.text: A thyristor waits for a gate pulse. The firing angle α is the delay, in electrical degrees, from the instant a diode in the same place would start conducting (the natural firing point) to the gate pulse. In single-phase circuits fed by vs = Vm sin ωt that point is the supply zero crossing: ωt = 0 for one device and π for the other.
Half-wave (one-pulse) circuit, R load. One thyristor conducts from α to π and turns off when its current falls to zero at π:
Vdc = (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α);   Vrms = (Vm/2)√[(π − α + ½ sin 2α)/π]
blocks.where: Vdc is the average and Vrms the RMS load voltage in V; Vm is the peak supply voltage in V; α is the firing angle.

blocks.text: RL load. The inductor carries current past π to the extinction angle β while the supply is negative, so Vdc = (Vm/2π)(cos α − cos β), less than the R-load value. The larger ωL/R, the later β and the nearer Vdc comes to zero; a freewheeling diode restores (Vm/2π)(1 + cos α).

RLE load (battery charging). With a back EMF E the thyristor is forward biased only while vs > E, that is between θ1 = sin⁻¹(E/Vm) and π − θ1. A gate pulse earlier than θ1 does nothing, so the firing range shrinks to θ1 < α < π − θ1.

sections.h3: Fully controlled bridge: two pulses, two quadrants

blocks.text: Four thyristors in a bridge: T1 and T2 form one diagonal and are fired at α; T3 and T4 form the other and are fired at π + α. The output has two pulses per cycle, so its ripple is at 2f. Each thyristor blocks Vm in both directions.
Vdc = (2Vm/π) cos α   (continuous current);   Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α)   (R load)
blocks.where: On a 230 V supply 2Vm/π = 207.07 V, the most the bridge can give.

blocks.text: With an R load the current stops at π, so the output is zero from 0 to α in each half-cycle. With a large inductance the current is continuous: T1 and T2 carry it past π until T3 and T4 are fired at π + α, so the output follows vs into its negative part. With RLE the averages obey Vdc = E + Idc R.

The current is continuous when the load inductance can carry it from one firing to the next. A large ωL/R helps; a large back EMF works against it, because E opposes the driving voltage and the current dies out sooner. When the current is discontinuous the output stops following the negative part of vs and rests at E (at zero for an RL load), so the actual Vdc is higher than (2Vm/π) cos α: the continuous-current formula under-predicts it.

Above α = 90° the formula gives a negative Vdc while the current keeps its direction, so power flows from the DC side to the AC supply. That needs a DC source in the load (a machine running as a generator, a reversed battery); an RL load alone cannot do it, since its average voltage is Idc R > 0. See inversion mode.

sections.h3: Half-controlled bridge and the freewheeling diode

blocks.text: The half-controlled (semi) bridge replaces two thyristors with diodes. When vs reverses, the load current freewheels through a thyristor and a diode in the same leg, so the output is clamped at zero. For R and RL loads Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α), never negative: one quadrant only. It needs two gate drives instead of four, and draws supply current only from α to π in each half-cycle, which raises the input displacement factor from cos α to cos(α/2).
A freewheeling diode across the load of a fully controlled bridge does the same job: the output is clamped at zero, Vdc = (Vm/π)(1 + cos α), and inversion is lost.

examples.question: A single-phase fully controlled bridge works from 230 V, 50 Hz with load resistance R = 10 Ω and α = 60°. Find Vdc and Idc (a) for a pure resistance and (b) with a large series inductance that makes the current continuous.
steps: (b) Continuous current: Vdc = (2Vm/π) cos 60° = 207.07 × 0.5 = 103.54 V; Idc = 103.54/10 = 10.35 A.
Why (b) is lower: from 180° to 240° T1 and T2 still conduct while vs is negative, adding a negative slice.

examples.question: A separately excited DC motor (armature R = 2 Ω, back EMF E = 100 V, large armature inductance) is fed from 230 V, 50 Hz at α = 45°. Find Vdc and Idc with a fully controlled bridge and with a half-controlled bridge. Assume continuous current.
steps: Check the power balance for the full bridge: Vdc Idc = 146.42 × 23.21 = 3398 W = E Idc + Idc²R = 2321 + 1077 W.
examples.answer: Full bridge 146.42 V and 23.21 A; half-controlled bridge 176.75 V and 38.38 A. The semi bridge gives more voltage at the same α because its output never goes negative.

traps: Using (2Vm/π) cos α for a pure resistance; with R it is (Vm/π)(1 + cos α).
Saying discontinuous current lowers Vdc below the cosine formula. It raises it: the negative slices disappear.
Claiming an RL load alone can make Vdc negative in steady state. Only a source in the DC circuit can.
Firing a battery charger before θ1 = sin⁻¹(E/Vm): the thyristor is still reverse biased and the pulse is lost.
Giving a half-controlled bridge a negative output. Its diodes clamp the output at zero.

quiz.q: Define the firing angle of a single-phase controlled rectifier.
quiz.a: The delay, in electrical degrees, from the natural firing point (the instant a diode in the same position would start conducting, here the supply zero crossing) to the gate pulse.

quiz.q: Why does the half-controlled bridge never give a negative average output?
quiz.a: When the supply reverses, the load current freewheels through a thyristor and a diode in the same leg, holding the output at zero. With no negative part the average can only fall to zero, at α = 180°.

quiz.q: A half-wave controlled rectifier runs from 230 V, 50 Hz with R = 20 Ω and α = 45°. Find Vdc and Idc.
A half-wave thyristor charger on 230 V, 50 Hz charges a 100 V battery. Within what range must α lie?
quiz.a: θ1 = sin⁻¹(100/325.27) = 17.9°. The thyristor is forward biased only from 17.9° to 180° − 17.9° = 162.1°, so 17.9° < α < 162.1°.

quiz.q: What does a freewheeling diode change in a fully controlled bridge with an RL load?
quiz.a: It clamps the output at zero whenever it would go negative, so Vdc becomes (Vm/π)(1 + cos α) instead of (2Vm/π) cos α. The supply current flows only from α to π, so the displacement factor improves, but the bridge can no longer invert.

quiz.q: For a fixed α and supply, what decides whether a bridge's current is continuous, and which way does Vdc move when it is not?
quiz.a: The load inductance must carry current from one firing to the next: large ωL/R helps, a large back EMF and a light load work against it. When the current is discontinuous the output rests at E (or zero) instead of following the negative supply, so Vdc is higher than (2Vm/π) cos α.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phase-controlled thyristor bridges remain the workhorse of large DC drives, electrolysis plants and HVDC terminals because they are robust and efficient, but new drives often use PWM active front ends that draw a sinusoidal current at unity power factor. Search for 'line-commutated converter', 'DC drive armature control' and 'active front end' next.

figure.caption: The worked example’s bridge at α = 60° on 230 V. With R alone (a) the output is zero until each firing, averaging 155.3 V; with a large inductance (b) T1 and T2 carry the current on until T3 and T4 fire at 240°, adding a negative slice and pulling the average down to 103.5 V.

spec.aria: Two plots against angle from 0 to 360 degrees with the supply sine dashed. Panel a, R load: output zero from 0 to 60 degrees, then the sine to 180, zero to 240, then the inverted sine; average 155.3 volts. Panel b, continuous current: the output follows the sine from 60 to 240 degrees including a negative slice after 180, then the inverted sine; average 103.5 volts. Firing marks at 60 and 240 degrees.
